headline: King tides hit California. A wave took part of a pier.
summary: King tides, the highest of the year, reached California this week. On Wednesday a wave tore part of the pier in Pacifica, south of San Francisco, into the ocean. Beachfront homes flooded. Waves of 20 to 30 feet were forecast for the Bay Area. San Diego's tide hit 8 feet 11 inches, likely a record, with a super El Niño pushing it higher.

cover_question.q: What makes a tide a king tide?

cover_answer: The moon and sun pulling together. The year's highest water.
table_question: Your favorite place is slowly flooding. Fix it, move it, or let it go?

5-7.script: The ocean in California came up very high this week, the highest it gets all year. One big wave knocked a piece of a long pier into the water, and some houses by the beach got wet inside. The waves were as tall as a two-story house. The pier was already closed, and the grown-ups are keeping people off the beach.
5-7.why: Two pictures they can see: a wave as tall as a house, a pier losing a piece. At five the ocean is a place, not a system, so the adults closing the beach matters most.
5-7.why_long: A five-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script gives them one wave as tall as a two-story house and one pier losing a piece, and lets them carry the event. Cantor found this age fears what looks dangerous, so the adults closing the beach is the line that matters. Expect 'can the ocean come to our house?' Not here.

8-12.script: The moon and the sun both pull on the ocean. A few times a year they line up, and the water rises higher than any other day: a king tide. This year a super El Niño warmed the Pacific, and warm water takes up more room. Think of a bathtub already full when someone climbs in.
8-12.why: Two pulls, a rise, a warm year, a pier gives. The bathtub makes the extra water real.
8-12.why_long: A child this age builds chains of cause and effect. This one is complete: two pulls line up, the water rises, a warm ocean takes up more room, so the year's highest tide came in higher still and took a pier with it. The bathtub makes the extra volume real. Expect 'will it happen again?' Yes, and more often as seas rise.

13-17.script: Who pays when the ocean takes a pier? Pacifica closed its pier in summer for cracks; a king tide finished it on Wednesday. San Diego broke a tide record set last month, and the BBC says king tides come more often as seas rise. Second: who decides when a beach house is too close?
13-17.why: Old physics, new records. Let them argue who should move first.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can reason about what is not in front of them, so the script runs two clocks: king tides are old physics, and the records they break are weeks old. It asks who pays for a pier already closed, then who decides when a house is too close. Expect 'is this climate change?' Partly. The El Niño is new. The rising sea is not.

5-7.q: Can the ocean come to our house?
5-7.a: No. Those houses sit right at the water's edge. The tide goes back out.

8-12.q: What makes a tide a king tide?
8-12.a: The moon and sun line up and pull together. The sea rises extra high.
Partly. Seas are rising, so king tides come more often.

13-17.a: The reports don't say. The city closed it in summer over cracks.

13-17.q: Why did San Diego's record fall twice in a month?
13-17.a: A super El Niño, the strongest on record, warmed the ocean.
